paras: The threatened lynching of William Price took place at Higginsville, Lafayette County, Missouri, in early March 1888, when, after Price, a Black man, was accused of cutting another man's neck in a saloon fight, there was talk among residents of lynching him. Officers quickly took Price out of town to the jail at Lexington, and no attempt on him was reported.

According to a local item in the Lexington Intelligencer, a "fraccas" at Higginsville on Monday, March 5, ended with Price, described as "a negro," cutting Robert Blakely severely about the neck. Physicians said that a very slight deviation of the knife would have cost Blakely his life. The paper's Higginsville correspondent gave a somewhat different account in the same issue: a "bad cutting scrape" at Fritz Bollwein's saloon on Tuesday, in which the bar keeper, whose name the writer had not learned, nearly lost his life at the hands of "a negro named William Price." That man lay in dangerous condition at the Arcade hotel.

Price "was very much condemned for the act," the Intelligencer wrote, and there was "serious talk among the citizens of giving him a dose of lynch law." For that reason officers quickly got him out of Higginsville, brought him to Lexington and put him in jail.
No report of an indictment or trial of Price, or of whether the wounded man recovered, was found in the coverage.

The episode appears only in the weekly Intelligencer of Lexington, the county seat, which ran the two items without headlines among local notes and advertisements. Both items identified Price by race; the shorts item gave the lynching talk as the reason for his quick removal, without comment, while the correspondent's letter did not mention it.

The two items differ on the day, Monday or Tuesday, and on the wounded man, whom one names as Robert Blakely and the other describes only as Bollwein's unnamed bar keeper. Both name William Price as the assailant in a near-fatal cutting at Higginsville that week, so they very likely describe the same incident, though the paper did not connect them.

No one was killed: A1 reports only talk among citizens of 'giving him a dose of lynch law' over the cutting, which led officers to move Price to the Lexington jail; no crowd or attack is described.
The only coverage is two items in one issue of the Lexington Intelligencer (A1); no other paper was found.

accounts.label: Intelligencer local item ('Shorts')
accounts.gist: A 'fraccas' at Higginsville last Monday ended with Price cutting Robert Blakely about the neck; with serious talk among citizens of lynch law, officers quickly took Price to the Lexington jail.

accounts.label: Higginsville correspondent
accounts.gist: A 'bad cutting scrape' at Fritz Bollwein's saloon on Tuesday nearly cost the bar keeper, whose name was not learned, his life at the hands of a negro named William Price; the wounded man was at the Arcade hotel and would be moved home to Sweet Springs. It says nothing about lynching talk.

framing.detail: The Intelligencer ran the episode as a brief local item without headline, identified Price as 'a negro', noted he 'was very much condemned for the act', and reported the lynching talk and the officers' removal without comment.

conflicts.note: Both items appear on the same page of A1; the shorts item says Monday, the Higginsville correspondent says Tuesday.

versions.value: the bar keeper at Fritz Bollwein's saloon, 'whose name we did not learn', whose home was at Sweet Springs

conflicts.note: The two items name the same assailant and a near-fatal cutting at Higginsville in the same week, so they very likely describe one incident, but the paper does not link them or confirm the bar keeper was Blakely.

info: The cutting took place 'last Monday' (March 5, 1888) per the shorts item, or 'Tuesday' (March 6, 1888) per the Higginsville letter, in the issue of Saturday, March 10, 1888.
Higginsville (printed 'Higginville' in one item), at the saloon of Fritz Bollwein per the Higginsville letter; Price was then jailed at Lexington.
William Price ('Wm. Price, a negro'), the man threatened with lynching.

Accused of cutting Robert Blakely severely about the neck with a knife in a 'fraccas'; the Higginsville letter says a bar keeper, name not learned, was cut by Price at Bollwein's saloon and nearly lost his life.
'The citizens' of Higginsville, among whom there was 'serious talk' of lynch law; no group is named or described as gathering.

Price was jailed at Lexington. The man he was accused of cutting (Robert Blakely in one item; an unnamed bar keeper in the other; race not given) lay at the Arcade hotel in dangerous condition. No report of an indictment, trial, or the wounded man's recovery or death was found.

sources.note: Two items on the local page: a 'shorts' item (Price cut Robert Blakely at 'Higginville' last Monday; serious talk of lynch law; officers took him to Lexington jail) and a Higginsville letter (cutting at Fritz Bollwein's saloon Tuesday; bar keeper, unnamed, nearly killed by a negro named William Price).
